before.title: Почему я сменил работу / Why I changed jobs
before.text:
Original teaching interview. Fictional speakers: interviewer Maya and guest Leo. Six listening blocks.

Block 1
Maya: You recently left your job at a furniture shop. Were you unhappy there?
Leo: Not really. I'd worked there for four years, and I liked the people. My manager was fair, too. I wasn't looking for a completely different life. I just wanted a working week that suited me better.

Block 2
Maya: What was the main difficulty?
Leo: The timetable. We usually got the next week's hours on Friday evening. I help my father with his shopping, so arranging that was difficult. At the new company, I get my timetable two weeks ahead. That makes planning much easier. It wasn't the number of hours that bothered me; it was finding out so late.

Block 3
Maya: Was there anything you wanted to learn?
Leo: Yes. In the shop, I answered questions about broken furniture, but someone else did the repairs. I wanted to learn how to repair things myself. My old manager understood, but there wasn't a training place available. My new job includes a training session every Wednesday morning. I haven't started those sessions yet, so I can't tell you how useful they are.

Block 4
Maya: And what about getting to work?
Leo: The shop was across town. The bus journey took about fifty minutes each way, sometimes longer. Now I can walk to work in twenty minutes. Getting that time back was my third reason for moving. The walk's quite pleasant, although I haven't tried it in heavy rain yet.

Block 5
Maya: Do you ever work from home?
Leo: The company has a trial arrangement for office tasks. My home day would be Tuesday—sorry, Wednesday. That's the day we discussed. But I can work from home one day a week only after my first month, if my manager agrees. It isn't automatic. On a home day, I'd join the morning training online and do customer messages afterwards.

Block 6
Maya: What would you tell someone thinking about a similar move?
Leo: Write down what you actually need. For me, it was earlier notice of my hours, a chance to learn repairs, and a shorter journey. I didn't leave because I disliked my colleagues. I still meet two of them for coffee. And a new job doesn't solve everything: I'm still learning the computer system, and that takes patience.

Block 1

Leo: Not really. I'd worked there for four years, and I liked the people. My manager was fair, too. I wasn't looking for a completely different life. I just wanted a working week that suited me better.

Block 2
Maya: What was the main difficulty?
Leo: The timetable. We usually got the next week's hours on Friday evening. I help my father with his shopping, so arranging that was difficult. At the new company, I get my timetable two weeks ahead. That makes planning much easier. It wasn't the number of hours that bothered me; it was finding out so late.

Block 3
Maya: Was there anything you wanted to learn?
Leo: Yes. In the shop, I answered questions about broken furniture, but someone else did the repairs. I wanted to learn how to repair things myself. My old manager understood, but there wasn't a training place available. My new job includes a training session every Wednesday morning. I haven't started those sessions yet, so I can't tell you how useful they are.

Block 4
Maya: And what about getting to work?
Leo: The shop was across town. The bus journey took about fifty minutes each way, sometimes longer. Now I can walk to work in twenty minutes. Getting that time back was my third reason for moving. The walk's quite pleasant, although I haven't tried it in heavy rain yet.

Block 5
Maya: Do you ever work from home?
Leo: The company has a trial arrangement for office tasks. My home day would be Tuesday—sorry, Wednesday. That's the day we discussed. But I can work from home one day a week only after my first month, if my manager agrees. It isn't automatic. On a home day, I'd join the morning training online and do customer messages afterwards.

Block 6
Maya: What would you tell someone thinking about a similar move?
Leo: Write down what you actually need. For me, it was earlier notice of my hours, a chance to learn repairs, and a shorter journey. I didn't leave because I disliked my colleagues. I still meet two of them for coffee. And a new job doesn't solve everything: I'm still learning the computer system, and that takes patience.

Check sheet: What did I hear? What is my hypothesis? Replay the short passage, then check the transcript. Record the evidence and explain the mismatch: word boundary, negative, cause, or correction. Исходная позиция — это положение до решения, включая положительные стороны, сомнения и ограничения. Она помогает не превращать спокойное объяснение в драматическую историю. Если человек сообщает о неудобстве, это ещё не означает, что он ненавидел свою работу. Отдельно фиксируйте событие и оценку: смена места работы является событием, а отношение к коллегам — оценкой.

changes.before:
Original teaching material — fictional club policy

Riverside Activity Club: cancelling a new membership

This page explains how to cancel a new membership and request a full refund. The same cancellation period applies to all new members. You do not need to give a reason. Read the steps carefully before sending your request: asking a general question is not the same as requesting cancellation.

Your cancellation request must reach the club by 6 p.m. local time on the fourteenth calendar day after your purchase. The day after purchase is day one. Calendar days include Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays. For example, if you buy a membership on 4 July, the deadline is 6 p.m. on 18 July. Requests received after the deadline do not qualify for a refund under this policy.

You must normally use the cancellation form in your online member account. Open “My membership”, choose “Cancel membership”, and complete the form. You must enter your full name, membership number and purchase date. Select “Cancel and request refund”, then press “Submit”. Simply opening or completing the form does not send a request. A successful request produces a confirmation email with a reference number.

Use the online form unless a technical problem prevents you from submitting it successfully. This is the only exception to the required submission method. If the form fails, you may send your cancellation request to cancellations@riverside.example instead. Your email must include the same three personal details and clearly say that you want to cancel and receive a refund. You must also describe the technical problem. The email must reach the club by the original deadline; a technical problem does not extend your cancellation period.

You should keep a copy of your request and any confirmation. You should check your inbox and spam folder. You may attach a screenshot of a technical problem, but a screenshot is not required. Staff review requests after they arrive, so the review itself may happen after your deadline. An eligible refund is returned to the original payment method within seven working days of approval. Here, working days mean Monday to Friday, excluding public holidays.

For help understanding these rules, contact help@riverside.example or speak to reception. Reception can explain the process, but a conversation or telephone call does not count as a cancellation request.

В интервью важно различать действие человека и результат команды. Местоимение I показывает вашу ответственность за конкретный шаг. Местоимение we показывает совместную работу или общий итог. Они не конкурируют: убедительный ответ часто содержит оба. Если несколько человек подготовили мероприятие, общий успех ещё не доказывает, что один кандидат руководил всеми. Выбирайте глагол по имеющимся фактам: helped означает участие, organised может означать организацию работы, а led прямо указывает на руководство. Замена helped на led делает рассказ сильнее только внешне и может исказить смысл.

Конкретный пример полезнее общей оценки вроде «я очень ответственный». Назовите действие, которое подтверждает качество, и дайте слушателю сделать вывод. При этом не придумывайте причинную связь. Если после вашего действия команда закончила работу, это не всегда означает, что именно вы обеспечили весь результат. Для осторожного описания подходят формулировки о том, чему действие помогло. Русское «мы сделали» также не следует автоматически переводить как I did, даже если рассказ посвящён вашему опыту.

Daniel, interviewer: Our neighbourhood group is discussing a traffic-free section of Willow Street. You helped organise last month's street afternoon, Maya. Before we get into the details, are you in favour of closing that section to cars?

Maya, guest: Yes, broadly. I think we give too much of our shared space to moving and parked vehicles. I would like people to be able to sit, talk, and cross the street without constantly watching for cars. That is my starting point, although supporting the idea is easier than designing a fair arrangement.

Daniel: What happened at the street afternoon that made the idea attractive to you?

Maya: The section between the library and the bakery was closed from two until six on a Sunday. We put out chairs, but we did not organise entertainment. People stayed anyway. One older resident, who usually crosses quickly and goes home, sat outside talking to two neighbours for nearly an hour. For me, that was a useful example of what the space could offer.

Daniel: So the event proved that a permanent closure would work?

Maya: No, it showed that people enjoyed one afternoon. It did not test an ordinary working day. The bakery had received its deliveries before the closure, and the weather was dry. We cannot assume those conditions would always apply. I would not use a pleasant Sunday as proof that every practical problem has been solved.

Daniel: The suggestion currently being discussed is six Saturdays, with the same section closed from ten in the morning until four. Is that what you support?

Maya: A limited trial seems reasonable, but I have become more cautious about the hours. A shop owner told me that some Saturday deliveries arrive after ten. That does not automatically defeat the proposal, but it means the timetable needs work. We need a workable delivery arrangement before the trial starts, not a promise to sort it out later.

Daniel: Imagine deliveries could all arrive before ten. Would you then recommend making the closure permanent immediately after the trial?

Maya: That is a possibility you are asking me to imagine, not something we have established. And even with deliveries arranged, I would still want a review. Six busy Saturdays might tell us something useful, but we should also ask who stopped coming and why. A crowded street can look successful while being inconvenient for people we no longer see.

Daniel: What would you include in that review?

Maya: Comments from residents and businesses, including people who disliked the trial, plus observations of traffic on nearby streets. Counting visitors alone would not be enough. I am not claiming that traffic will increase elsewhere; I am saying we should check. Someone also needs to explain how those findings will influence the next decision.

Daniel: Has the council approved the trial or announced a starting date?

Maya: Neither. This is still a neighbourhood proposal. The council has not approved it, and there is no announced starting date. Our group can recommend an approach, but we cannot authorise a road closure ourselves.

Daniel: Then give us your final position in one sentence.

Maya: I support trying a temporary closure, provided there is a workable delivery arrangement and a clear review plan before it begins; I am not supporting an immediate permanent closure.

Daniel: And what would you ask neighbours to do now?

Maya: Describe specific needs and difficulties, rather than simply voting for a cheerful picture or against any change. I still like the idea. I just want our enthusiasm to lead to a proposal we can actually evaluate.

changes.before:
Original teaching material: a fictional community thread.

Post 1 — Lena, learner
I support recording our evening classes because my work sometimes prevents me from arriving on time. Last Tuesday I missed the explanation of the writing task and spent the break trying to reconstruct it. That was frustrating, especially because nobody had done anything wrong. I want access to instructions, not a collection of other people's mistakes. Could we separate the tutor's explanation from the discussion? This would help people like me without turning every contribution into something permanent.

Post 2 — Omar, learner
Lena's distinction matters. However, knowing that a recorder is running can change what people are willing to say. I sometimes test an idea before I believe it, which is part of learning for me. If that unfinished thought can be replayed, I may stay quiet. My priority is a space where we can take intellectual risks. Recording only explanations sounds better than recording everything, but I would need to understand exactly when the recorder stops.

Post 3 — Beth, volunteer organiser
I hear a shared wish to protect learning, although you are describing different kinds of access. Lena needs access after the event; Omar needs freedom during it. We should also consider how a recording is found. A folder full of unnamed files would not solve Lena's problem. I propose a clear title and a short description for each recording. This is a usability proposal, not an argument for recording more of the class.

Post 4 — Daniel, tutor
Beth's suggestion would make the archive easier to navigate. Still, a recording of an explanation is not necessarily a complete explanation: sometimes the useful clarification comes from a learner's question later. That is why I hesitate to promise that recordings can replace attendance. I can see their value as an additional resource. Any policy should describe what the files contain and what learners will still need to ask about, rather than presenting the archive as a complete course.

Post 5 — Mina, community editor
The useful question seems to be what should be recorded and for what purpose. I suggest that learners post examples of moments they would want to revisit, without naming classmates. That would give us concrete needs to discuss. Meanwhile, anyone who misses instructions should contact the tutor through the course page. This is something members can do now, before the community settles the recording policy. Please respond to the proposals rather than guessing one another's motives.

Original teaching material: a fictional vacancy and candidate profile.

MAPLE ROOM: COMMUNITY COORDINATOR

Maple Room is a small neighbourhood community with around seventy registered members. It organises reading circles, repair evenings and informal skill exchanges. The coordinator will write clear activity reminders, maintain registration lists, welcome new members and pass difficult questions to a committee member. The role involves four hours of work per week, normally on weekday evenings. The description does not say whether those hours are fixed or arranged each week.

Applicants should provide one concrete example of organising information or communicating with a group. Formal management experience is not required. Accuracy matters more than impressive claims. The coordinator will use a shared spreadsheet and email account. The committee makes policy decisions. The start date and payment for the coordinator's work will be discussed with shortlisted applicants.

ALEX: AGREED CANDIDATE FACTS

Alex volunteered at three repair evenings over two months. A team of four volunteers organised the events. Alex created a shared registration sheet, checked it before each event and sent reminder emails two days beforehand. Alex also answered routine questions about times and directions. Another volunteer booked the room; the team leader assigned practical tasks and dealt with complaints.

Across the three evenings, forty people attended in total. The team did not measure whether Alex's reminders increased attendance or reduced missed bookings. Alex has used basic spreadsheet functions but has never collected membership payments or managed a budget.

Alex is interested in helping neighbours participate. Alex can regularly offer four hours between 18:00 and 21:00 on weekdays, with at least three days' notice. Weekend availability has not been established. These facts define the experience available for this application; no additional achievements should be assumed.

Original teaching material. The neighbourhood, project, device and all figures below are fictional.

[1] The Alder Quay community project has installed one small particle sensor beside the entrance to its shared courtyard. The pilot is intended to help residents notice local patterns and identify periods worth investigating. It is not designed to certify that the neighbourhood meets a legal standard. The public display reports an estimated concentration of fine particles, labelled PM2.5, near the device. PM2.5 refers to a category of very small airborne particles, approximately 2.5 micrometres in diameter or smaller.

[2] Inside the sensor, a fan draws air through a chamber containing a light source. Particles scatter the light, and the instrument uses that signal to estimate particle concentration. It does not collect and weigh every particle. Its conversion assumes certain particle properties, so a different mixture can change the relationship between scattered light and estimated mass. The displayed unit is micrograms per cubic metre: an estimated mass of particles within a volume of air. The device does not identify the chemical composition of the particles or measure gases such as nitrogen dioxide.

[3] The instrument produces a reading each minute. Every fifteen minutes, the display updates with the arithmetic mean of the valid minute readings from the preceding fifteen-minute block. A displayed value of 18 therefore does not mean that every minute had a value of 18. A brief higher reading may be partly hidden by lower readings within the same block. At least twelve valid minute readings are required for a block to appear. If fewer are available, the display shows a dash. A dash means insufficient data, not an absence of particles.

[4] During the project's preliminary comparison with a reference instrument, fifteen-minute estimates were usually within 5 micrograms per cubic metre of the reference values when concentrations were between 10 and 40. Those checks took place with relative humidity below 75 percent and a clean air inlet. This is a description of those checks, not a guaranteed error limit for every future reading. At higher humidity, water associated with particles can increase light scattering and make estimates higher. The project has not established a reliable correction for that effect.

[5] The installation needs an unobstructed inlet, a working fan and protection from direct rain. A coordinator checks the inlet weekly and records interruptions. A reading marked with a maintenance flag should be reviewed before it is used in a comparison. The sensor describes air near its inlet, not conditions in every street, home or room. Wind direction and nearby activities may affect the reading. A change can justify looking for explanations, but the number alone cannot identify which activity caused it.

[6] For public explanations, the project recommends beginning with what the number represents, then stating its time period and its limits. Comparisons are most informative when the location, averaging period and operating conditions are comparable. A repeated pattern across comparable periods provides a stronger basis for investigation than one isolated difference. Even then, the display does not provide a complete assessment of air quality or an individual's exposure. It supplies one limited piece of environmental information. Questions about causes require additional observations; questions about compliance require an appropriate assessment beyond this pilot.

Original teaching material. The film, people and events described below are fictional.

The Space Between Notes: listening beyond the music

A chair scrapes across a rehearsal room before anyone plays a note. In Mara Ellison’s documentary The Space Between Notes, that small interruption establishes the film’s most productive habit: listening to the work around a performance. Following a neighbourhood orchestra as it prepares one concert, Ellison finds drama in decisions that a polished recording would normally conceal. Her film is strongest when it makes those decisions audible, and less convincing when it treats shared enthusiasm as an answer to practical difficulties.

The central figures are conductor Leila Grant and volunteer organiser Ben Cole. Grant wants longer rehearsals to give inexperienced players confidence; Cole worries that extra evenings will exclude members with other commitments. Ellison introduces their disagreement without assigning either person the role of villain. This matters because the film’s argument depends on recognising that participation and artistic ambition can compete even when everyone involved is acting in good faith.

Its finest sequence begins with the orchestra attempting the same short passage three times. The camera stays wide enough to include a violinist lowering her instrument while the brass section works. We hear whispered counting, a cough and Grant’s increasingly precise instructions. Instead of telling us that collective music requires patience, the film lets us experience how unevenly that patience is distributed. The sequence is slow, but its duration earns its place: the waiting is part of the subject.

Ellison is equally alert to what editing can suggest. A close shot of Cole folding rehearsal notices is followed by players discussing whether they can attend another session. The connection makes administrative work visible without turning the organiser into a martyr. There is a risk of sentimentality in the accompanying piano score, yet the concrete task keeps the moment grounded. We see labour, not merely a label announcing community spirit.

The interviews are more limited. Grant is allowed to develop her ideas about musical quality, whereas two players who cannot manage additional rehearsals appear only in brief exchanges. Their reasons are mentioned but not explored. As a result, the film shows that scheduling creates friction without giving that friction the same intellectual attention as the conductor’s artistic goals. This is an imbalance of treatment, not evidence that Grant is personally indifferent to the players.

A late montage of smiling faces encourages us to feel that the group has found a workable balance. That emotional movement is understandable, but the film has not established whether the new arrangements remain manageable beyond this concert. Warmth supplies a sense of resolution that the evidence cannot fully support. The distinction matters: a successful evening and a sustainable organisation are related achievements, but they are not interchangeable.

None of this cancels the documentary’s achievement as an account of rehearsal. Ellison gives ordinary pauses a clear expressive purpose and allows reasonable positions to collide. The result invites discussion about whose time makes a collective project possible, even where its own discussion becomes selective. It is a perceptive film with a narrower argument than its reassuring final movement suggests.

For readers who enjoy documentaries about creative work, especially those involved in amateur arts groups, this is worth seeking out for its patient attention to process. Readers looking for a practical guide to running an inclusive orchestra should expect observations rather than solutions. Its most valuable offering is a better question to bring to the next rehearsal, not a ready-made policy.

Her film is strongest when it makes those decisions audible, and less convincing when it treats shared enthusiasm as an answer to practical difficulties.

The central figures are conductor Leila Grant and volunteer organizer Ben Cole. Grant wants longer rehearsals to give inexperienced players confidence; Cole worries that extra evenings will exclude members with other commitments. Ellison introduces their disagreement without assigning either person the role of villain. This matters because the film’s argument depends on recognizing that participation and artistic ambition can compete even when everyone involved is acting in good faith.

Its finest sequence begins with the orchestra attempting the same short passage three times. The camera stays wide enough to include a violinist lowering her instrument while the brass section works. We hear whispered counting, a cough and Grant’s increasingly precise instructions. Instead of telling us that collective music requires patience, the film lets us experience how unevenly that patience is distributed. The sequence is slow, but its duration earns its place: the waiting is part of the subject.

Ellison is equally alert to what editing can suggest. A close shot of Cole folding rehearsal notices is followed by players discussing whether they can attend another session. The connection makes administrative work visible without turning the organizer into a martyr. There is a risk of sentimentality in the accompanying piano score, yet the concrete task keeps the moment grounded. We see labor, not merely a label announcing community spirit.

The interviews are more limited. Grant is allowed to develop her ideas about musical quality, whereas two players who cannot manage additional rehearsals appear only in brief exchanges. Their reasons are mentioned but not explored. As a result, the film shows that scheduling creates friction without giving that friction the same intellectual attention as the conductor’s artistic goals. This is an imbalance of treatment, not evidence that Grant is personally indifferent to the players.

A late montage of smiling faces encourages us to feel that the group has found a workable balance. That emotional movement is understandable, but the film has not established whether the new arrangements remain manageable beyond this concert. Warmth supplies a sense of resolution that the evidence cannot fully support. The distinction matters: a successful evening and a sustainable organization are related achievements, but they are not interchangeable.

None of this cancels the documentary’s achievement as an account of rehearsal. Ellison gives ordinary pauses a clear expressive purpose and allows reasonable positions to collide. The result invites discussion about whose time makes a collective project possible, even where its own discussion becomes selective. It is a perceptive film with a narrower argument than its reassuring final movement suggests.

For readers who enjoy documentaries about creative work, especially those involved in amateur arts groups, this is worth seeking out for its patient attention to process. Readers looking for a practical guide to running an inclusive orchestra should expect observations rather than solutions. Its most valuable offering is a better question to bring to the next rehearsal, not a ready-made policy.

Original teaching material. All names, institutions, scenes and events in this dossier are fictional.

Film and setting

After the Counter is a seventy-two-minute documentary directed by Nessa Vale. It follows the fictional town of Bellwick during a six-week trial of a new booking system at its public repair workshop. The workshop offers staffed repair benches for residents’ household items. Under the trial, most appointments must be reserved online; a small number remain available through a reception desk. The film observes the trial without announcing whether it becomes permanent.

Four scenes

First, workshop coordinator Amira Shah demonstrates the booking page before opening time. She explains that advance descriptions of faults help staff prepare tools. The camera then follows her searching for a tool needed for an unexpected repair.

Second, resident Peter Lowe reaches reception with a broken lamp. He has tried the online form but cannot identify the required repair category. The receptionist helps him complete the booking. The scene shows a difficulty with the categories, not an absence of internet access.

Third, Shah and Lowe examine a printed timetable together. She points to fewer interruptions during booked sessions. He points to the effort required before anyone reaches a workbench. Neither withdraws their position, and the scene ends without an agreement.

Fourth, the camera watches a repair session from a fixed position. Several benches are occupied while one remains empty. No explanation is given for the empty bench, and the people using the others are not presented as a representative sample.

Form and positions

Vale uses long observational takes, close shots of forms and tools, and no explanatory voice-over. Shah argues that preparation protects staff time and improves the work they can offer. Lowe accepts the value of planning but argues that booking should not require residents to diagnose their own objects. The dossier provides no budget figures or measured comparison of access before and after the trial.

Magazine commission

Frame & Forum is a magazine for readers interested in documentary craft and the organisation of public services. Its editor requests a critical review that connects formal choices to the film’s argument, treats both participants fairly and gives a useful viewing recommendation. Readers are comfortable with basic film terminology. Use only this dossier as evidence about the film.

What should residents need to know before booking a repair?

Bellwick’s public repair workshop provides staffed benches where residents can bring household items. During a six-week trial, most appointments were booked online, with a small number available through reception. The documentary After the Counter follows the trial and raises a practical question: how much must users understand before they can ask for help?

Resident Peter Lowe tries the online form but cannot select the right repair category for his lamp. A receptionist helps him book. His experience concerns the form’s categories, so it would be misleading to describe him as unable to get online.

Coordinator Amira Shah offers another perspective. Knowing about faults in advance helps staff prepare tools, and she points to fewer interruptions during booked sessions. Planning can therefore address a real staff concern while still requiring effort from residents.

The film does not establish whether access improved overall. One resident’s difficulty and an unexplained empty bench cannot settle that question. It also provides no budget figures from which to judge savings. Residents can recognise both concerns without assuming the trial has succeeded or failed.

What help will the workshop provide when someone cannot identify the repair category they need?

Editorial note: I replaced specialist language about film form with an explanation of the workshop, making the article accessible without prior viewing. I corrected the claim about Lowe’s internet access and removed assertions about savings, changing unsupported factual meanings. I also replaced the dismissive description of his objections with a concrete account of his difficulty. Finally, the closing question serves residents’ needs instead of promoting the film.

The Harbour Museum is preparing a small exhibition about a neighbourhood printing club. The central object is issue four of the club's magazine, published in 1986. Here, issue identifies one edition, not a difficulty requiring action. The curator's opening address will introduce the volunteers who preserved the collection. It should last no more than three minutes.

A preview involved eighteen invited visitors. Twelve stayed for the entire demonstration, while six left before it ended. The departures suggest that the format may need attention, but they do not establish boredom: two visitors mentioned a bus departure, and nobody interviewed the other four.

The museum wants the demonstration to be a memorable experience, not a test of visitors' printing experience. The editor must prepare a short public description and a private recommendation. The public text should explain the event without presenting uncertain interpretations as facts. The private recommendation should distinguish the required briefing from the unapproved proposal.

The museum context changes several lexical decisions. In the pilot, an issue would be a problem requiring attention; in the exhibition, issue four identifies a countable magazine edition. Address also changes role: addressing missing dates means dealing with a problem, whereas the curator's opening address is a countable formal speech. Suggest introduces a recommendation in the pilot, using suggest doing or suggest that someone do something. changes.before:
Original teaching material: a fictional short story.

The Last Key

By six, the rain had erased the opposite bank of the river. I had promised the council that the reading room would be empty by seven. After thirty years as its keeper, I could surely be trusted with one final evening. The notice on the door said CLOSED, though I had turned it inward. There was no reason to make the street look more deserted than it was.

I was counting the returned keys when Mara arrived. Three lay beside the register; the fourth was in my waistcoat pocket. It opened the narrow cupboard behind the lending desk, where her mother's notebooks had been kept since the exhibition. Mara carried a cardboard box with handles cut into its sides. I remember thinking that she had chosen something practical. Later, she said I had laughed at it.

'I came for the notebooks,' she said.

'You came rather late.'

'You told me after six.'

That was possible. I had been answering questions all week: where the chairs would go, whether the children's height marks would be painted over, who owned the clock. Precision becomes difficult when everyone mistakes a building for a person who can be persuaded to stay.

I opened the register to her mother's donation. The agreement was quite clear: the notebooks were to remain available for public consultation while the reading room operated. If it closed permanently, the donor or her named representative could reclaim them. Mara's name appeared beneath her mother's, in smaller writing. The council called this closure permanent. I had hoped the word might prove premature.

'Until the collection has been checked, nothing should leave,' I said.

'Is that in the agreement?'

I laid a finger along the page, not on any particular sentence. What I meant was that things disappear when they travel. Her mother had understood this. She used to bring loose pages in shopping bags and leave with them arranged in folders. I supplied the folders. I do not think it unreasonable to mention that.

Mara put the box on the desk. Its bottom was lined with a folded towel. I had imagined the notebooks knocking against one another in the boot of her car; the towel embarrassed me, though I cannot have shown it. She asked for the key. I touched my pocket to check that it was safe.

'It isn't among the returned ones,' I said.

This was accurate. Accuracy is not always as helpful as people expect.

Outside, a van reversed towards the entrance. Its warning sounded three times and stopped. Mara looked at the cupboard, then at the three keys. 'We can wait,' she said. I took this as an accusation that I was making her wait. Perhaps it was merely an offer. At the time, offers had begun to sound like instructions.

For a moment, consider the room from Mara's side of the desk. An old man stands between her and a cupboard. He has just touched his pocket. On the page below his hand, her own name authorises her to collect what she requested. There is a towel in her box, but he has explained how easily things can be damaged. She cannot hear the sentences in which he has been generous for thirty years.

I can give her that view now. I did not ask for it then.

Instead, I said her mother had wanted the notebooks read. Mara answered that she had arranged a table at the neighbourhood centre for Saturday. She would bring them there each month. I asked whether anyone qualified would supervise. Her mother had been a bus driver who wrote about birds during her breaks. I had never asked who qualified her to notice them.

Mara took an envelope from her coat. 'She left instructions for me as well.'

I did not reach for it. I knew her mother's handwriting on the front, but not what was inside. It would be convenient to say that I feared some private grief. In fact, I feared a sentence that would make my assistance unnecessary. I am less certain whether admitting this now makes the rest of my account more trustworthy.

The van driver knocked. He wanted the desk first, while there was still light. I told him to take the chairs. Mara sat on the nearest one before he could lift it. Neither of us smiled. The clock, which had been five minutes slow all winter, struck seven.

I brought out the fourth key and placed it beside the others. Mara did not pick it up. 'You can open it,' she said. There was no forgiveness in the words that I could recognise, but recognition was never my strongest service to that family.

At the cupboard I hesitated, listening for the soft scrape of the box being lifted. Behind me, paper moved. Perhaps Mara had opened the envelope; perhaps she had only moved the register out of the driver's way. The key entered easily. I turned it until something yielded, and waited to discover whether I had opened the door.

Original teaching material: a fictional dramatic adaptation.

A reading room on its final evening. A desk, three keys, a register, a locked cupboard. ELIAS, the keeper, stands behind the desk. Before MARA enters, he takes a fourth key from the cupboard lock and pockets it. He straightens the register. Rain.

MARA: You said after six.

ELIAS: I thought you might telephone.

MARA: I brought a box.

She places it on the desk. A towel lines the bottom. ELIAS reaches towards the towel, then withdraws his hand.

ELIAS: Your mother wanted people to read them.

MARA: They can. At the neighbourhood centre.

ELIAS: Can they?

MARA: On Saturdays. I've arranged a table.

ELIAS: And someone to watch it?

MARA: Someone will be there.

She opens the register and turns it towards him.

MARA: Permanent closure. Named representative. Here.

ELIAS: I know what it says.

MARA: Then we need the key.

ELIAS: It isn't among those.

A pause. MARA looks at the keys. ELIAS looks at her box.

MARA: The centre needs confirmation by seven. Otherwise they'll give the table to someone else.

ELIAS: You didn't tell me.

MARA: I'm telling you now.

A reversing alarm sounds outside. MARA takes an envelope from her coat and places it, unopened, beside the register.

ELIAS: Is that for me?

MARA: It has my name on it.

He puts his hand in his pocket. A knock interrupts him.

DRIVER, outside: Desk first?

ELIAS: Chairs.

MARA sits on a chair. The DRIVER does not enter.

ELIAS: Your mother never minded waiting.

MARA: She minded being called patient.

Original teaching material: a fictional dramatic adaptation.

A reading room on its final evening. A desk, three keys, a register, a locked cupboard. ELIAS, the keeper, stands behind the desk. Before MARA enters, he takes a fourth key from the cupboard lock and pockets it. He straightens the register. Rain.

MARA: You said after six.

ELIAS: I thought you might telephone.

MARA: I brought a box.

She places it on the desk. A towel lines the bottom. ELIAS reaches towards the towel, then withdraws his hand.

ELIAS: Your mother wanted people to read them.

MARA: They can. At the neighborhood center.

ELIAS: Can they?

MARA: On Saturdays. I've arranged a table.

ELIAS: And someone to watch it?

MARA: Someone will be there.

She opens the register and turns it towards him.

MARA: Permanent closure. Named representative. Here.

ELIAS: I know what it says.

MARA: Then we need the key.

ELIAS: It isn't among those.

MARA: The center needs confirmation by seven. Otherwise they'll give the table to someone else.

ELIAS: You didn't tell me.

MARA: I'm telling you now.

A reversing alarm sounds outside. MARA takes an envelope from her coat and places it, unopened, beside the register.

MARA: It has my name on it.

He puts his hand in his pocket. A knock interrupts him.

ELIAS: Chairs.

MARA sits on a chair. The DRIVER does not enter.

MARA: She minded being called patient.

Silence. He places the fourth key on the desk. She leaves it there.

MARA: You can open it.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. Fictional interview script for locally synthesised speech.

Host, Mara: The council wants to redesign Foundry Square, moving its central stone and putting recorded memories along the surrounding walls. You advised the early discussions, although you are not on the design team. In a sentence, do you support the proposal?

Guest, Ellis: In a sentence, I support making the square more usable without making its past easier to misunderstand. If you mean the current proposal, my answer is no, not as it stands. Moving the stone is being presented as a practical adjustment, almost like moving a bench. But the position of an object can be part of what it tells us. I would want the council to explain that loss before asking us to celebrate the gain. That is not a demand that every object remain exactly where somebody first put it.

Mara: The Access Note says the present route is difficult for some wheelchair users. Are you putting historical meaning ahead of access?

Ellis: No. The note identifies a narrow turn beside the stone, and I take that seriously. What I have not seen is a comparison showing that moving the stone is the only workable response. The note records the difficulty; it does not choose a design. Those are different jobs. I would be perfectly willing to examine a relocation scheme that preserves a legible connection with the original position. I am resisting the idea that accepting the problem commits you to this particular solution.

Mara: What would a legible connection actually look like?

Ellis: It might include a visible outline on the ground, an explanation at the new position, and a route between them that people can follow. But please do not turn those possibilities into my approved specification. I have not checked whether they would work here. There is a temptation, in these discussions, to treat an example as a signature. Someone asks what might help; you answer; the next document says the adviser supports the design. An illustration of a principle is not a professional assessment of a finished plan.

Mara: You sound rather wary of the documents.

Ellis: Of what documents get asked to do, perhaps. My mother used to work in the old ticket office beside the square. Years after it closed, she saw an exhibition caption describing the office as a place where neighbours exchanged stories. She said, yes, sometimes, but mostly we sold tickets and tried to keep the rain off the accounts. I remember being disappointed. I wanted her workplace to have been a little theatre of community life. She wanted someone to remember the leaking roof. Neither version was entirely false, but one was much easier to put on a cheerful panel. I mention that because selection can become sentiment without anybody consciously deciding to mislead.

Mara: Does that make the proposed recorded memories a problem too?

Ellis: Potentially, though let me come back to your question about documents first. I trust the Access Note as a record of the obstacle its author observed. I do not treat it as permission for every alteration that follows. Likewise, the Memory Catalogue tells us what has been collected, not what the whole neighbourhood remembers. It lists eighteen recorded contributions, eleven from former shopkeepers. That may produce excellent material. It cannot, on those numbers alone, justify the phrase “the community's voice”. We do not know from the catalogue how people were approached or who declined.

Mara: The project officer calls it a first collection, not a representative sample.

Ellis: Then that is a useful distinction, and the public description should keep it. My concern is that careful language tends to disappear between the working document and the launch banner. “A first collection” becomes “our shared memory”, and suddenly a limited invitation has acquired a very large hat. Forgive the expression, but it matters. I would welcome the recordings as attributed individual accounts, provided visitors can see how the collection was assembled and how further contributions can be offered.

Mara: Suppose those explanations were included and the original position remained clearly marked. Would you still oppose moving the stone?

Ellis: I would no longer oppose relocation in principle on historical grounds. That is narrower than saying I would approve this design. Access, maintenance and the actual quality of the interpretation would still need assessment. Earlier I said my answer to the proposal was no. More precisely, my answer to presenting it as ready for approval is no. There may be a defensible proposal inside it; I am not yet persuaded that the necessary work has been done.

Mara: So a headline saying you have changed your mind would be fair?

Ellis: It would be tidy. Fair is another matter. You have made the conditions more explicit, and I have made the scope of my objection more explicit. If that counts as changing my mind, the phrase needs quite a lot of furniture around it. I am less concerned with keeping my opening sentence intact than with keeping the decision open until its basis is clear.

Mara: What should listeners ask for next?

Ellis: A revised proposal that separates the access problem, the relocation options and the claims made for the recordings. Publish the reasoning connecting them. Then people can disagree about an actual choice rather than being told that concern for access or respect for memory leaves only one answer. I would be glad to take part in that discussion. I would not want my willingness to discuss it advertised as an endorsement.

Mara: Our editor read your line about no longer opposing relocation in principle as permission to say you support a trial move. Is that what you meant?

Mara: There is also an update. The team has sent a revised drawing showing an outline at the original position. Can we report that your main condition has now been met?

Ellis: You can report what the drawing shows, if you have checked it. I have not seen it. An outline alone would not tell me whether visitors could understand the relationship between the positions. Please do not use my earlier hypothetical answer as an assessment of a drawing I have not reviewed.

Ellis: I can clarify my words now, but I cannot assess the revision tonight. I would need the drawing and its explanatory text. My request for a transparent account of the recordings also remains. I am not withdrawing the conditional openness I expressed. I am saying that conditional openness and approval are different statements.

changes.before:
Регистр — выбор языковых средств с учётом отношений, аудитории и задачи. Форум допускает короткие реплики и разговорные выражения; официальный итог требует точных глаголов, ясных субъектов и осторожного описания поддержки. Задача модератора — сделать смысл доступным всем, сохранив серьёзность интересов. Не нужно копировать раздражённый тон участника или превращать каждую реплику в канцелярский документ.

Особенно важны глаголы полномочий. Recommend означает рекомендовать, approve — утвердить, authorise — разрешить действие в пределах компетенции, implement — осуществить. Русское «мы решили» легко превращается в We have decided, хотя группа могла лишь согласовать рекомендацию. Такая замена создаёт ложное обязательство и меняет институциональный смысл разговора.

Общие критерии позволяют сравнивать предложения без оценки личности. Критерий должен иметь наблюдаемое содержание: например, понятность процедуры можно проверять по тому, смог ли новый пользователь самостоятельно завершить необходимые шаги. Слово fair само по себе ещё не критерий. На уровне C2 важно также признать конфликт критериев: повышение предсказуемости может ограничить гибкость. Модератор не обязан скрывать этот конфликт ради приятного итога; его задача — сделать основания выбора понятными и проверяемыми.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. Fictional forum, Stage 1. Read this stage before opening later stages.

Mara, volunteer coordinator: We need a recommendation for Saturday access. All six workstations are currently booked online. Volunteers say the queue at opening time is difficult to explain to people without reservations.

Leila, access representative: My concern is the person who discovers the workshop on Saturday morning. An apparently public facility can feel closed if every useful opportunity disappeared online several days earlier.

Owen, regular user: Sure, but I carry a repair project across town. If I cannot reserve a station, I could spend an hour travelling just to turn straight back round.

Jules, board liaison: The board has requested a proposal for a four-Saturday pilot, with reasons. It has not asked us to prove that either reservations or arrival-based access is universally superior.

Mara: From the volunteer side, one understandable procedure matters. Explaining six different exceptions while helping people use tools is not a realistic way to begin a busy session.

Leila: Some people always manage to get a place. We need to look at what makes access easier for them and harder for somebody approaching the system for the first time.

Owen: The booking calendar does provide certainty. I check it during my lunch break, and knowing I have a station helps me decide which materials are worth bringing.

Jules: Could we distinguish the availability of a place from the visibility of the procedure? A published system may still require knowledge that an experienced user no longer notices.

Leila: Exactly. A newcomer may not know when bookings open, whether a cancelled place returns to the calendar, or whom to ask if the screen is confusing on a phone.

Mara: Those are questions we can explain more clearly. However, clearer instructions alone will not create extra stations, so our recommendation must also describe how we allocate limited space.

Owen: I could consider a mixed arrangement. What I would need is a meaningful opportunity to reserve, rather than a nominal booking option that almost never produces an available place.

Jules: And any mixed arrangement needs an evaluation method. Counting occupied stations would tell us something about use, but very little about the people who tried and failed to attend.

Leila: I would want unsuccessful attempts included. A full room is not sufficient evidence of accessible provision if we never hear from the people who could not get through the process.

Mara: We can record enquiries and refusals without collecting people's personal stories. I would also want volunteers to report how much explanation the arrangement requires during an ordinary session.

Owen: That sounds reasonable as evidence. I am still unsure how much reserved time a mixed arrangement would offer, and I would like that specified before supporting a particular version.

Jules: Then the immediate task is to describe the interests accurately and identify what remains unspecified. A recommendation will be stronger if participants can recognise their own concerns in it.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. Fictional governance note available from Stage 1.

Harbour Community Workshop has six workstations. Its Saturday public session runs from 16:00 to 19:00. Under the current arrangement, users reserve stations online. Participants in this forum are discussing a four-Saturday pilot; no alternative arrangement has been approved.

Mara coordinates volunteers. She can estimate workload and draft instructions, but cannot change building access rules. Leila represents an access group and can report concerns and support proposals; she cannot claim to speak for every newcomer. Owen contributes the perspective of a regular user and has no allocation authority. Jules carries recommendations to the board but cannot approve them on its behalf. The learner acts as forum moderator and has no independent decision-making power.

The board must approve a pilot before it begins. Any proposal must explain allocation, user information, volunteer demands and evaluation. Existing safety requirements continue to apply. This discussion cannot alter workshop fees.

Potential evaluation criteria include predictability, ease of understanding, unsuccessful attempts to attend and volunteer workload. These are matters to define together, not agreed measures yet. Participants may support a trial while reserving judgement about a permanent arrangement.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. Fictional forum, Stage 2. Open only after completing the Stage 1 tasks.

Owen: I have been thinking about Leila's line, 'Some people always manage to get a place.' It sounds as though I am being accused of working the system. I follow the published procedure. I do not want my attendance treated as evidence against me.

Leila: I was not alleging that you cheated or received favours. I meant that familiarity can make the same procedure easier to use. I can see that 'manage' did not make that distinction clear. I still want us to examine the procedure.

Owen: I appreciate that distinction. I need to know whether the recommendation will discuss barriers in the process or suggest that frequent users themselves are the problem. Those would be very different accounts of this conversation.

Jules: Let us check that meaning explicitly before drafting the account. We should neither attribute an accusation Leila denies nor assume Owen's concern has disappeared because an explanation has been offered.

Mara: On allocation, here is a possible compromise: make 16:00 to 17:00 arrival-based, then offer two bookable periods, 17:00 to 18:00 and 18:00 to 19:00. All six stations would follow that pattern. It would give volunteers one procedure to explain.

Leila: I could support testing that shape if arrival-based access is explained clearly and unsuccessful attempts are recorded. It would give a newcomer some opportunity without advance online booking.

Owen: I could support that provisionally too, assuming people with later reservations can arrive when their reserved period begins. I still want confirmation of how the report will represent my concern.

Jules: This is a candidate recommendation, subject to checking feasibility and board approval. Neither has happened yet.

changes.before:
To the Workshop Board
Subject: Conditional recommendation for a four-Saturday access pilot

The forum identified overlapping but distinct aims. Leila seeks a realistic route in for people unfamiliar with booking; Owen needs predictable access to justify travelling with materials. Mara needs a procedure volunteers can operate, while Jules needs a proposal the board can assess.

An ambiguous comment about people obtaining places was heard by Owen as questioning his conduct. Leila denied alleging cheating or favours and clarified that her concern was familiarity with the process. Owen acknowledged the distinction but requested accurate representation. This report therefore examines procedural barriers without characterising regular attendance as wrongdoing.

The revised proposal would offer arrival-based access at all six stations from 16:00 to 17:00, with registration at the door, followed by bookable periods from 17:00 to 18:00 and 18:00 to 19:00. For entry after 17:00, users must appear on the attendance list submitted by 15:00 on Friday. Booking closure must allow that submission. An unlisted replacement cannot enter after 17:00 merely because a reservation has been cancelled.

Owen supports a trial provided these conditions are prominent before booking. Leila supports it only on the explicit basis that spontaneous evening access remains unavailable, including for people finishing work at 17:00. Her support does not endorse the arrangement as equitable. Board approval remains necessary; fees are outside this discussion's remit.

Mara can draft instructions, and Jules can submit the proposal. Capacity to record unsuccessful attempts consistently remains unconfirmed. Whether building access arrangements could change after the pilot is also unknown.

The trial could inform assessment of predictability, clarity and workload. However, full occupancy alone would not demonstrate accessibility. The board should request a feasible evaluation plan and preserve the unresolved evening-access issue when considering approval.

Исправьте два подготовленных текста. Сначала выполните A по m1–m4. Вариант B сохраните для отсроченного повторения через 24–48 часов: вся необходимая информация уже дана ниже. Это один тип задания с двумя отдельными случаями; не переносите правила мастерской в случай B.

A. Адресат — совет мастерской. Цель — заменить недостоверный итог точной, профессиональной запиской. Напишите исправленный итог объёмом 150–180 английских слов, затем объясните по-английски две существенные смысловые или регистровые правки ещё в 40–60 словах. Полный неудачный оригинал, авторский учебный материал:

"The forum has settled the access dispute and approved the new Saturday system. Leila admitted that her criticism of regular users was unfair, and Owen accepted her apology. Original teaching material. The magazine, project, people and events below are fictional.

At Margin, our small cultural magazine, we have been discussing the Lantern Rooms, a proposal to turn a disused station office into a place for exhibitions and recorded neighbourhood memories. The drawings are attractive. So is the promise that visitors will encounter the district through its residents rather than through a developer's preferred adjectives. Whether the building can support that promise is a less photogenic question.

Mara, the project's organiser, wears her heart on her sleeve. When she describes the listening benches, her hands travel around an imaginary room, stopping wherever a visitor might sit. This makes her persuasive, but it also makes her easy to underestimate. Enthusiasm is sometimes treated as evidence that a person has forgotten the drains. Mara has obtained a drainage survey. She brings it to meetings in the same folder as her sketches.

Our reviews editor, Ellis, likes both the sketches and the survey. His objection concerns the collection of memories. An early leaflet promised to recover a particular recording of a station porter singing. Nobody can identify the person who supposedly made it. Ellis calls the search a wild-goose chase. Mara replies that three residents remember hearing the song, although none claims to have heard that recording. She has now removed the promise from the leaflet and given the search a two-week limit.

Both positions deserve more than their shortest description. Ellis is protecting a modest budget from a story that becomes more expensive whenever it becomes more charming. Mara thinks a limited search can uncover other useful material even if the advertised treasure never appears. She has already found a timetable annotated by a former cleaner. It is not the recording, but it complicates the assumption that nothing worth finding lies along an uncertain route.

The argument becomes less attractive when we discuss attention. Another local project has received a prominent review, and somebody around our table invokes the green-eyed monster to explain the Lantern team's impatience. It is an efficient little diagnosis: no interview required, no inconvenient distinction between wanting praise and wanting an answer. The team has, in fact, been waiting for a decision about access to the station office. That does not make envy impossible. It does make envy an oddly complete explanation.

Ellis worries that our eventual feature will become a campaign brochure. Mara worries that a preference for scepticism will be mistaken for independence. She points out that we routinely describe abandoned plans as failures, then treat anyone still pursuing a plan as insufficiently realistic. Ellis answers that persistence cannot make every cost defensible. Neither is arguing nonsense. Their disagreement concerns when sympathy should become commitment, and what evidence ought to make that transition possible.

At Tuesday's meeting, the project committee approved the room layout, the volunteer rota and the launch date in one fell swoop by adopting a single motion. Several people welcomed the speed. I did too, initially. There is something comforting about a table at which three difficult matters become one manageable sentence. The minutes record unanimous agreement. They do not record whether anyone asked how volunteers would supervise the listening equipment while guiding visitors through the exhibition.

This may be an omission in the minutes rather than in the discussion. Still, our editor admired the document's remarkable tidiness: a question absent from the record could no longer delay the schedule. We laughed, and then moved on to choosing a photograph. I am less certain now that the joke was directed entirely at the committee. Our own efficient meeting had also found a way to leave an awkward question without an owner.

Funding is not a foregone conclusion. The committee has submitted an application, and the building owner has offered temporary access, but neither fact supplies the missing money. I want the Lantern Rooms to open. I also want our feature to distinguish that wish from a prediction. A magazine can recognise affection without treating it as a business plan, and recognise doubt without awarding it automatic intellectual superiority. If our familiar expressions help us draw those distinctions, they have earned their space. If they settle the argument before the evidence arrives, they are merely very well-dressed shortcuts.

Original teaching dialogue. This is a scripted rehearsal involving fictional editors and responses, not a live conversation. Read this stage only when directed to open it.

Nina: The preview of our column has reached a different audience. A neighbourhood translation group shared it with new residents. Their coordinator says several readers understand the individual words but do not recognise the literary expressions. We cannot assume that a Shakespeare reference supplies its own explanation.

Ellis: Agreed, although removing every image would flatten the column. The argument is partly about how images guide judgement. Readers should be able to encounter an unfamiliar expression without being treated as incapable of understanding it.

Nina: There is also a specific complaint. Jo, a Lantern volunteer, wrote to us after seeing the preview. The quotation card beside the jealousy paragraph names Jo and reproduces her question: 'Why has the access decision taken six weeks?' She says the placement makes the monster metaphor look like our explanation of her behaviour.

Ellis: The column actually challenges that explanation. The reference to waiting for access is meant to expose its weakness. But someone reading the card and the opening of the paragraph could reasonably connect the label to Jo. The layout changes the apparent target.

Nina: Jo wants the public record to make clear that we have no evidence about her motive. She has not asked us to endorse the project or remove criticism of its budget. We should not turn her complaint into a demand she never made.

Ellis: Nor should we announce that nobody on the team could possibly feel envy. We do not know that either. We can explain what our evidence concerns and what it cannot establish.

Nina: Then our clarification needs to address the placement and preserve the distinction between support and certainty. It must stand alone on the preview page. Readers should not need the whole column or a reference book to follow it.

Ellis: Let's retain one literary connection only if we explain its present meaning. Elsewhere, describe the issue directly. The objective is an accountable clarification, not a vocabulary test or a defence of our cleverness.

changes.before: These five expressions are attested in Shakespeare's plays, but the references do not establish that he invented them. Their historical settings can illuminate an image without determining every modern use. Today, a foregone conclusion is an outcome regarded as already settled, not simply a conclusion reached earlier. The Lantern committee's application therefore does not make funding a foregone conclusion: the money remains uncertain. In one fell swoop describes accomplishing several things through one action, and it need not imply disaster. In Macbeth, Act 4, scene 3, the expression concerns the death of Macduff's family; in the column, it describes approving three arrangements through a single motion. That procedural fact does not itself establish either catastrophe or good judgement. Readers need a clear account of the present meaning, not complete knowledge of the dramatic scene. Our note should make the language accessible while keeping the project's practical uncertainties visible.

changes.before:
An idiom is useful when it gives a thought shape, not when it merely gives a writer something recognisable to display. Saying that someone wears her heart on her sleeve can make emotional openness visible in a way that an administrative description cannot. The image invites us to imagine a person whose feelings are available to others. Whether that openness is admirable still depends on the surrounding argument.

There is a reasonable objection to excessive caution. If editors replace every inherited expression with a neutral explanation, cultural writing may lose rhythm, humour and the pleasure of recognition. Readers can also enjoy learning an unfamiliar phrase. Accessibility need not mean eliminating surprise.

The difficulty begins when an image supplies a judgement that the evidence has not earned. Imagine a fictional museum newsletter describing a volunteer's attempt to identify an unsigned photograph as a wild-goose chase. The volunteer has searched for only an afternoon and has already located the correct decade. A reader might reasonably conclude that the work is pointless, although the available facts establish only that identification is unfinished. Here the idiom saves words by spending more certainty than the writer possesses.

A better edit would describe the limited progress and explain why further searching may or may not be worthwhile. The expression could remain in a quotation if the surrounding text examined that judgement instead of silently adopting it.

Literary history adds another pleasure, provided we label it accurately. An expression's presence in Shakespeare establishes a connection worth exploring, not automatic proof of his invention. Good cultural writing lets inherited language sharpen attention while remaining answerable to present evidence.

Original teaching report. Greyhaven, its residents, and all local observations and figures below are fictional.

At Greyhaven's western edge, the River Lerr widens into an estuary before meeting the sea. The town occupies its southern shore. A paved quay runs east from the river mouth to Bell Head, a headland projecting beyond the neighbouring shoreline. Beyond this headland, the coast faces open water. Inside the estuary, a wetland lies between the quay's western end and a shallow creek. Farther offshore, east of Bell Head, a small platform carries instruments, although its readings are not included in the current project papers.

These places are connected, but they do not behave identically. Near the creek, river water mixes with seawater, producing brackish water whose salinity varies. The tide raises and lowers water levels along the waterfront. A current can also carry suspended sediment through the estuary. On a windy afternoon, a visitor watching floating leaves may notice movement without being able to identify its cause. The open beach beyond Bell Head receives different exposure from the sheltered inner shore, so a description of one location cannot automatically represent the other.

The council is considering two approaches to a worn section of waterfront. One would retain the quay's present line and replace a damaged section of seawall. The other would move part of the paved route inland, leaving more room beside the wetland and providing a lower terrace closer to the water. Both are discussion options, rather than approved construction plans. The second option's preliminary description assumes that the terrace would remain above ordinary high tides and therefore offer daily access. Neither option comes with a promise that every future flood would be prevented.

Mara Venn, who runs a repair shop near the quay, supports keeping the present line. Her strongest argument concerns continuity: the existing promenade connects homes, shops and the public square without a detour. She worries that moving the route would weaken that connection and make the waterfront feel less public. A renewed seawall, she argues, could protect the land immediately behind it while retaining a familiar walking route. However, she accepts that a wall does not create more beach, and she wants the council to explain what would happen at its ends.

Jon Hale, a volunteer with the town's habitat group, prefers moving part of the route inland. He argues that the wetland needs space as water and sediment conditions change. A fixed boundary can restrict the area into which a shoreline habitat might shift. He also sees the proposed terrace as a way to keep people close to the estuary rather than separating them from it. Jon acknowledges that relocation would use some existing paved public space. His support depends on the replacement route being genuinely useful, not merely appearing as a thin line in a proposal.

The available observations are modest. Over eight months, volunteers repeatedly measured the shoreline position at six marked sections of the open beach beyond Bell Head. Four sections showed a net landward movement; the largest recorded change was 0.4 metres. Two showed a small net gain of beach material. These results document local change during that period, not a long-term rate for the whole coast. No sediment-tracking study established whether material lost from one section reached either of the sections that gained it.

Council records also list three temporary closures of the western quay during high tides accompanied by strong winds. Those entries do not include measurements separating the normal tidal level from any additional storm-related rise. Original teaching report. Greyhaven, its residents, and all local observations and figures below are fictional.

At Greyhaven's western edge, the River Lerr widens into an estuary before meeting the sea. The town occupies its southern shore. A paved quay runs east from the river mouth to Bell Head, a headland projecting beyond the neighboring shoreline. Beyond this headland, the coast faces open water. Inside the estuary, a wetland lies between the quay's western end and a shallow creek. Farther offshore, east of Bell Head, a small platform carries instruments, although its readings are not included in the current project papers.

These places are connected, but they do not behave identically. Near the creek, river water mixes with seawater, producing brackish water whose salinity varies. The tide raises and lowers water levels along the waterfront. A current can also carry suspended sediment through the estuary. On a windy afternoon, a visitor watching floating leaves may notice movement without being able to identify its cause. The open beach beyond Bell Head receives different exposure from the sheltered inner shore, so a description of one location cannot automatically represent the other.

The council is considering two approaches to a worn section of waterfront. One would retain the quay's present line and replace a damaged section of seawall. The other would move part of the paved route inland, leaving more room beside the wetland and providing a lower terrace closer to the water. Both are discussion options, rather than approved construction plans. The second option's preliminary description assumes that the terrace would remain above ordinary high tides and therefore offer daily access. Neither option comes with a promise that every future flood would be prevented.

Mara Venn, who runs a repair shop near the quay, supports keeping the present line. Her strongest argument concerns continuity: the existing promenade connects homes, shops and the public square without a detour. She worries that moving the route would weaken that connection and make the waterfront feel less public. A renewed seawall, she argues, could protect the land immediately behind it while retaining a familiar walking route. However, she accepts that a wall does not create more beach, and she wants the council to explain what would happen at its ends.

Jon Hale, a volunteer with the town's habitat group, prefers moving part of the route inland. He argues that the wetland needs space as water and sediment conditions change. A fixed boundary can restrict the area into which a shoreline habitat might shift. He also sees the proposed terrace as a way to keep people close to the estuary rather than separating them from it. Jon acknowledges that relocation would use some existing paved public space. His support depends on the replacement route being genuinely useful, not merely appearing as a thin line in a proposal.

The available observations are modest. Over eight months, volunteers repeatedly measured the shoreline position at six marked sections of the open beach beyond Bell Head. Four sections showed a net landward movement; the largest recorded change was 0.4 meters. Two showed a small net gain of beach material. These results document local change during that period, not a long-term rate for the whole coast. No sediment-tracking study established whether material lost from one section reached either of the sections that gained it.

Council records also list three temporary closures of the western quay during high tides accompanied by strong winds. Those entries do not include measurements separating the normal tidal level from any additional storm-related rise. A wetland survey identified feeding birds and small fish in the creek margin, but covered only two visits in one season. It provides evidence of habitat use, not a complete annual picture. No option has yet been tested against all the conditions residents have raised.

The disagreement is therefore partly about priorities and partly about missing connections in the evidence. Mara asks how access can be maintained along the waterfront; Jon asks what kind of shore will remain beside that access. Both want public space to survive. Before choosing, residents need to distinguish what has been seen from what is expected, and ask whether each expectation is supported at the particular place where it matters.

Original teaching reference. All examples are invented and describe no real project.

1. Coast: the broader zone where land meets the sea. Use along the coast when discussing several locations. Example: Conditions vary along this coast.

2. Shoreline: the boundary between land and water at a particular time or under a stated convention. Example: The survey recorded a change in shoreline position.

3. Estuary: typically, a partly enclosed coastal area where river water and seawater meet. Freshwater estuaries also exist, so mixed salinity is not universal. Example: The river widens into an estuary.

4. Brackish water: water with salinity between freshwater and seawater. Brackish describes salt content, not cleanliness. Example: Brackish water fills the creek after seawater enters.

5. Headland: land extending out into the sea beyond the adjacent coast. Example: The beach continues beyond the rocky headland.

6. Offshore: situated in the sea away from the shore, or directed away from it. Distance needs separate wording. Example: Instruments operate two kilometres offshore.

7. Tide: the regular rise and fall of water level driven mainly by lunar and solar gravity. Example: The tide rises during the afternoon.

8. Current: a directed flow of water. Tides, wind and density differences can drive currents. A tidal current is one kind. Example: A current carries sediment towards the inlet.

9. Storm surge: the storm-related increase above the predicted astronomical tidal level. It is an additional rise, not the complete level. Example: The storm surge added half a metre to the predicted level.

10. Storm tide: the resulting water level when the astronomical tide and storm surge combine. Compare levels using the same reference point. Example: The reported storm tide included both contributions.

11. Sediment: particles such as sand or silt that water can transport and deposit. Erosion removes material; deposition leaves it elsewhere. Example: Sediment accumulated where the flow slowed.

12. Seawall: a wall intended to protect coastal land from water and wave action. Its wider effects depend on local conditions. Example: The proposal retains the seawall beside the square.

13. Wetland: land that remains wet or is regularly flooded, supporting associated habitats. Some coastal wetlands can retain part of incoming runoff. Example: The wetland provides feeding habitat beside the creek.
